content.prompt: Part 1 — The thief meets Anil
content.answer: The story is narrated by a young thief who is about fifteen years old. He is an experienced crook: he changes his name whenever he changes his work. One day, he meets a young man called Anil, who is watching a wrestling match. The narrator flatters him, pretending to be a wrestler's trainer, and Anil, a generous and trusting man, invites him home. The thief notices that Anil is easy to rob — he earns money from odd writing work and spends it quickly, living a simple, casual life. The narrator plans to stay with Anil, win his trust, and then rob him.

content.prompt: Part 2 — Living with Anil
content.answer: The thief lives with Anil, cooking and helping about the house. Anil teaches him to write his name, and later promises to teach him to write whole sentences and add numbers. He is a kind, carefree master who is content with small earnings and simple living. The narrator, meanwhile, keeps looking for a chance to rob him. Anil pays him daily for his work, but the thief soon realises that Anil's friendship and trust mean more to him than money — a feeling that makes him uneasy, because he is, after all, a thief with a reputation to maintain.

content.prompt: Part 3 — The theft
content.answer: One evening, Anil brings home a small bundle of notes — his payment for an article sold to a magazine. He puts it under his mattress. That night, when Anil is asleep, the thief steals the money and slips out of the room. He has a moment of triumph as he counts the notes in the moonlight. But then a strange thing happens: he feels cold and lonely, and the money no longer gives him the happiness he expected. He walks the streets, lost in thought, and decides to return the notes to Anil's bed before morning.

content.prompt: Part 4 — The new start
content.answer: The thief creeps back and places the money under the mattress, then lies down, tense and afraid. The next morning, Anil wakes him. The thief fears he has been discovered, but Anil, though he knows the notes have been returned — "a little too damp" from being handled — says nothing about the theft. He simply tells the boy that he will now teach him to write whole sentences. The thief is overwhelmed: Anil's forgiveness and trust have changed his life. He has lost his fear of being caught, and gained something better — the wish to be honest. The story ends with the boy smiling at the rain, ready to begin learning.

content.prompt: The power of trust and kindness
content.answer: The central theme is the transforming power of trust and kindness. Anil's simple trust in the thief — teaching him, treating him as a friend, and forgiving him without a word — changes the boy more than any punishment could. Trust gives the thief a reason to be honest; kindness makes him feel he belongs. The story shows that people can change when they are treated with respect, and that redemption often comes not from fear but from love.

content.prompt: Money versus human values
content.answer: The story contrasts money with human values. The thief is drawn by the pleasure of money, but when he steals Anil's earnings, he finds the money brings him no joy — only coldness and loneliness. What he really craves is Anil's friendship and respect, which are worth more than any notes. The theme shows that material wealth cannot satisfy the human heart; relationships, trust and self-respect are the real treasures.

content.prompt: Redemption and second chances
content.answer: The story is about redemption and second chances. The young thief, hardened by a life of crime, is given a chance to change by Anil's quiet generosity. His decision to return the money, and Anil's silent forgiveness, open a new path for him — a life of learning and honesty. The theme suggests that no one is beyond redemption, and that a single act of trust can turn a life around.

content.prompt: The narrator (the young thief)
content.answer: The narrator is a fifteen-year-old thief who is skilled and confident in his trade. He changes his name with each job and sizes up his victims cleverly — he sees that Anil is "easy to rob" because he trusts people. Yet beneath the crook's facade is an uneasy boy: Anil's friendship and teaching make him feel something he has never felt, and stealing from him brings no happiness, only loneliness. His decision to return the money and his joy at Anil's forgiveness show his growth — he is capable of change when offered trust. He is intelligent, observant and, at heart, not as hard as his profession suggests.

content.prompt: Anil
content.answer: Anil is a young, easy-going writer who lives simply, earning money from odd assignments and spending it quickly. He is generous and trusting: he takes the stranger home, feeds him, teaches him to write and pays him daily. His most remarkable quality is his quiet wisdom — when he discovers the theft, he says nothing, only comments that the notes were damp, and instead offers to teach the boy to write whole sentences. Anil's trust and forgiveness are the instruments of the thief's change. He represents the power of quiet kindness: he does not lecture, he simply gives the boy a reason to be honest.

content.prompt: The narrator's inner self (the boy beneath the thief)
content.answer: Though the narrator hides behind the identity of a practised thief, the story slowly reveals the boy beneath: someone who has never been trusted, loved or taught. His uneasiness when Anil pays him, his disappointment in himself when stealing brings no joy, and his final decision to return the money all show a conscience long dormant. He is proud (he boasts of being a clever thief), vulnerable (Anil's kindness unsettles him) and finally hopeful. This inner character — loyal, hungry for affection, capable of honesty — is the real subject of the story, and it is his awakening that the narrative traces.

content.prompt: Trust can change a person
content.answer: The story teaches that trust and kindness are more powerful than suspicion and punishment. Anil's trust in the thief — and his silent forgiveness when the money is returned — transforms the boy's life. The lesson is that people respond to respect: when we believe in someone's goodness, we give them the strength to become good.

content.prompt: Honesty brings true happiness
content.answer: The thief's brief joy in the stolen money turns to coldness and loneliness, while his decision to return it leads to peace and hope. The story teaches that ill-gotten wealth cannot satisfy us, and that honesty — and the self-respect it brings — is the only durable source of happiness.

content.answer: The narrator is a young, unnamed thief, about fifteen years old, who changes his name with each new job.

content.answer: The thief met Anil at a wrestling match and flattered him by pretending to be a trainer, winning his trust and an invitation home.

content.answer: Because Anil was trusting, earned only small amounts from odd writing work and spent his money quickly, leaving none to guard.

content.answer: He said the notes were "a little too damp" after the thief returned them, showing he knew without accusing him.

content.answer: He offered to teach the thief to write whole sentences, giving him a new start and a reason to be honest.

content.prompt: How did Anil's trust change the thief?
content.answer: Anil's trust worked a quiet revolution in the thief. When they met, the thief was a practised crook who planned to rob Anil at the first opportunity. But Anil treated him with simple generosity: he fed him, taught him to write his name, paid him daily and made him a companion. The thief, who had never been trusted, began to value that trust — he even felt uneasy when Anil paid him, because "friendship" was new to him. When he finally stole the money, he found it brought him no happiness, only loneliness, because he had robbed the one person who had believed in him. His return of the money, and Anil's silent forgiveness — expressed in his remark that the notes were damp, and in his offer to teach him more — gave the thief something richer than any theft: a chance to be honest, and the wish to deserve Anil's trust. The story shows that trust can redeem where punishment would only harden.

content.prompt: What does the story teach us about money and happiness?
content.answer: The story teaches that money alone cannot bring happiness. The thief's profession was built on the idea that money is the only prize worth having, and when he stole Anil's notes, he expected triumph. Instead, he felt "cold" and "lonely", and walking the streets with the money gave him no pleasure. His happiness returned only when he chose to give the money back and be trusted again. The lesson is that material wealth is hollow without human values — friendship, trust, self-respect and honesty. The thief's real poverty was not the lack of money but the lack of these things, and Anil's friendship filled that poverty. True contentment, the story suggests, comes not from what we take, but from what we give and become.

content.prompt: Value question: Is the thief's change believable? Justify with evidence from the story.
content.answer: Yes, the thief's change is believable because it is gradual and psychologically true. The thief is not a hardened monster but a boy — about fifteen years old — who chose crime for survival and habit. From the start, the story plants seeds of change: he notices that Anil is kind, he enjoys learning to write his name, and he feels "uneasy" about his own feelings because they clash with his identity as a thief. The decisive moment comes when the stolen money brings him no joy — this shows his conscience awakening. His return of the notes is not sudden saintliness but a longing to keep Anil's friendship, which has become more valuable to him than money. Finally, Anil's quiet forgiveness — knowing and yet not accusing, and still offering to teach him — provides the love and trust that make honesty possible. The boy's smile in the rain shows his genuine hope. Change may be rare, but the story makes it credible: trust, not punishment, gave him a reason to become good.

content.prompt: Describe Anil's character. How does he differ from the thief?
content.answer: Anil is an easy-going young writer, generous, trusting and content with a simple life. He earns money from odd assignments, spends it quickly and cares little for possessions or security. He is also quietly wise: he recognises the boy's need for guidance and teaches him to write, and when he discovers the theft, he does not rage or punish — he makes a gentle remark about the damp notes and offers continued teaching, giving the boy his trust once more. The thief, in contrast, is watchful, calculating and hardened by a life of crime — he plans, lies and sizes people up for their weaknesses. Yet the difference between them shrinks as the story progresses: Anil's humanity awakens the boy's own, and in the end, the thief begins to take after Anil — learning, trusting, and smiling at the rain. Anil differs from the thief in his values: he is rich in trust and generosity, while the boy was rich only in tricks.

content.prompt: Why does the thief say Anil would be "out of work" if he were caught? What does this reveal?
content.answer: The thief says that if Anil were caught stealing, he would be out of work because he "could not make a living by theft" — a joke, but a revealing one. It shows the thief's admiration for Anil's honest simplicity, and his own sly awareness of their difference: Anil could never survive as a crook because he lacks the cunning and the hunger. The remark also reveals the narrator's growing affection — he measures the world by Anil's goodness. More deeply, it hints at his internal conflict: he knows his own trade is dishonourable, and he admires the man he plans to rob. This self-aware humour makes the thief likeable and prepares the reader for his change, because he already knows, in his heart, that Anil's life is the better one.
